concept_summary: IOS-XR uses a commit-based configuration model where changes are staged and must be explicitly committed to take effect. Initial setup includes hostname, domain configuration, management interface addressing, and user creation. Unlike IOS/IOS-XE, configuration changes are not applied immediately but are validated and committed as a transaction, allowing rollback if needed.
cli_mode_context: Enter configuration mode with 'configure' or 'config' command. Make configuration changes, then use 'commit' to apply them. Use 'show configuration' to view uncommitted changes before committing.
example_commands:
configure
hostname PE-Router01
domain name example.com
interface MgmtEth0/RP0/CPU0/0
 ipv4 address 192.0.2.10 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
username admin
 group root-lr
 group cisco-support
 secret Str0ngP@ss
banner motd ;
Authorized Access Only - PE-Router01
;
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR interface naming includes location identifiers showing rack/slot/module/port position. Interfaces require explicit IPv4/IPv6 address family configuration. Sub-interfaces support dot1q encapsulation for VLAN tagging. Interface configuration follows the commit model requiring explicit commit after changes.
cli_mode_context: Enter interface configuration with 'interface <type><location>' where location format is Rack/Slot/Instance/Port (e.g., 'interface TenGigE0/0/0/1'). Configure address families explicitly.
example_commands:
configure
interface TenGigE0/0/0/1
 description Core-Uplink-to-P1
 ipv4 address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.252
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8::1/127
 no shutdown
interface TenGigE0/0/0/2.100
 description Customer-A-VLAN100
 encapsulation dot1q 100
 ipv4 address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
interface Loopback0
 description Router-ID
 ipv4 address 192.0.2.100 255.255.255.255
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR handles Layer 2 services primarily through L2VPN constructs rather than traditional VLAN switching. Bridge domains provide Layer 2 forwarding within a router, while L2VPN services like VPWS and VPLS extend Layer 2 connectivity across MPLS networks. Sub-interfaces with dot1q encapsulation handle VLAN tagging at Layer 3 handoffs.
cli_mode_context: Configure bridge domains with 'l2vpn bridge group <name> bridge-domain <name>'. For simple VLAN sub-interfaces, use 'interface <int>.<vlan>' with 'encapsulation dot1q <vlan-id>'.
example_commands:
configure
l2vpn
 bridge group BG-METRO
  bridge-domain BD-CUST-100
   interface TenGigE0/0/0/1.100
   interface TenGigE0/0/0/2.100
   routed interface BVI100
interface BVI100
 ipv4 address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.0
interface TenGigE0/0/0/1.100 l2transport
 encapsulation dot1q 100
 rewrite ingress tag pop 1 symmetric
interface TenGigE0/0/0/2.100 l2transport
 encapsulation dot1q 100
 rewrite ingress tag pop 1 symmetric
commit
end

concept_summary: Static routes provide explicit forwarding paths to destination networks. IOS-XR supports both IPv4 and IPv6 static routes with next-hop addresses or exit interfaces. Administrative distance can be adjusted to prefer or deprioritize static routes relative to dynamic protocols. VRF-aware static routing is supported for multi-tenancy.
cli_mode_context: Configure static routes under 'router static' configuration mode. Specify address family (ipv4 or ipv6) and VRF context if applicable.
example_commands:
configure
router static
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  0.0.0.0/0 192.0.2.1
  198.51.100.0/24 TenGigE0/0/0/1
  203.0.113.0/24 192.0.2.5 5
  203.0.113.128/25 Null0 description Blackhole
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  ::/0 2001:DB8::1
vrf CUSTOMER-A
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  10.0.0.0/8 198.51.100.1
commit
end

concept_summary: OSPF in IOS-XR operates as a link-state IGP with area hierarchy and SPF path calculation. Configuration uses a process-name rather than process-ID, and interfaces are explicitly added to areas. IOS-XR supports both OSPFv2 for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6, with advanced features like NSR for hitless failover and graceful restart for control-plane resilience.
cli_mode_context: Configure OSPF with 'router ospf <process-name>' and explicitly assign areas to interfaces. Use 'area <area-id>' context to configure area parameters.
example_commands:
configure
router ospf CORE
 router-id 192.0.2.1
 nsr
 area 0
  interface Loopback0
   passive enable
  interface TenGigE0/0/0/1
   network point-to-point
   cost 10
 area 10
  interface TenGigE0/0/0/2
commit
end

concept_summary: BGP in IOS-XR is a path-vector protocol for inter-domain routing with extensive policy control through Routing Policy Language. IOS-XR BGP supports multiple address families (IPv4, IPv6, VPNv4, VPNv6, EVPN) and advanced features like route reflection, confederation, and graceful restart. Configuration uses hierarchical structure with neighbor groups and session groups for scalability.
cli_mode_context: Configure BGP with 'router bgp <as-number>' and define neighbors under 'neighbor <ip>' context. Apply policies with RPL using 'route-policy' statements. Activate address families explicitly.
example_commands:
configure
route-policy PASS-ALL
 pass
end-policy
router bgp 65001
 bgp router-id 192.0.2.1
 address-family ipv4 unicast
 address-family vpnv4 unicast
 neighbor 198.51.100.1
  remote-as 65002
  description EBGP-to-ISP
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   route-policy PASS-ALL in
   route-policy PASS-ALL out
 neighbor 192.0.2.254
  remote-as 65001
  update-source Loopback0
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   next-hop-self
  address-family vpnv4 unicast
commit
end

concept_summary: IS-IS is a link-state IGP commonly deployed in service provider networks due to its scalability and protocol-independent design. IOS-XR implements IS-IS with both IPv4 and IPv6 support in single-topology or multi-topology mode. IS-IS uses NET addresses for router identification and operates at Layer 2, making it independent of IP addressing. Configuration supports flexible metrics, authentication, and multi-level hierarchy.
cli_mode_context: Configure IS-IS with 'router isis <tag>' and assign NET address. Enable IS-IS on interfaces explicitly. IOS-XR focuses on IS-IS rather than EIGRP for IGP requirements.
example_commands:
configure
router isis CORE
 is-type level-2-only
 net 49.0001.0192.0000.2001.00
 address-family ipv4 unicast
  metric-style wide
 address-family ipv6 unicast
  metric-style wide
 interface Loopback0
  passive
  address-family ipv4 unicast
  address-family ipv6 unicast
 interface TenGigE0/0/0/1
  point-to-point
  address-family ipv4 unicast
   metric 10
  address-family ipv6 unicast
   metric 10
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR supports VRRP for first-hop redundancy, providing virtual IP gateway services with automatic failover. Multiple routers share a virtual IP address with one acting as master based on priority election. VRRP ensures continuous connectivity for end hosts when individual routers fail. IOS-XR implementation follows RFC 5798 with support for IPv4 and IPv6.
cli_mode_context: Configure VRRP under interface context with 'router vrrp' commands. Specify virtual IP and adjust priority for master election.
example_commands:
configure
interface TenGigE0/0/0/5.10
 description Customer-Facing-VLAN10
 encapsulation dot1q 10
 ipv4 address 192.0.2.2 255.255.255.0
 router vrrp 1
  address 192.0.2.1
  priority 110
  preempt delay minimum 60
interface TenGigE0/0/0/5.20
 description Customer-Facing-VLAN20
 encapsulation dot1q 20
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:10::2/64
 router vrrp 1 version 3
  address-family ipv6
   address global 2001:DB8:10::1
   priority 110
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR uses IPv4 and IPv6 ACLs for traffic filtering with sequence numbers for precise ordering. ACLs can match on Layer 3/4 parameters including addresses, protocols, ports, and flags. Hierarchical naming and object groups provide better manageability. ACLs are applied to interfaces or used in policy contexts like routing policy or QoS classification.
cli_mode_context: Define ACLs with 'ipv4 access-list' or 'ipv6 access-list' followed by name. Apply to interfaces in ingress or egress direction with 'ipv4 access-group' in interface configuration.
example_commands:
configure
ipv4 access-list BLOCK-TELNET
 10 remark Block Telnet access
 20 deny tcp any any eq telnet log
 30 permit ipv4 any any
ipv4 access-list PERMIT-MGMT
 10 permit tcp 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq ssh
 20 permit tcp 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq https
 30 deny ipv4 any any log
interface TenGigE0/0/0/10
 ipv4 access-group BLOCK-TELNET ingress
ipv6 access-list BLOCK-v6
 10 deny ipv6 any any fragments
 20 permit ipv6 2001:DB8::/32 any
 30 deny ipv6 any any log
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR supports Network Address Translation for IPv4 address conservation and translation between private and public address spaces. NAT44 provides static, dynamic, and PAT functionality. Configuration includes defining inside/outside interfaces, NAT rules with address pools, and optional port translation. Service provider deployments often use NAT at customer edge or in CGN scenarios.
cli_mode_context: Configure NAT under 'service nat44' or 'router nat' context depending on platform. Define rules and pools, then apply NAT instance to interfaces.
example_commands:
configure
interface TenGigE0/0/0/1
 service-policy type pbr NAT-POLICY
nat44 inside
nat44 outside
nat44 pool PUBLIC-POOL 198.51.100.1 198.51.100.10
nat44 rule INSIDE-TO-OUTSIDE
 source-prefix 192.0.2.0/24
 destination-prefix 0.0.0.0/0
 pool PUBLIC-POOL
 overload
nat44 rule STATIC-MAP
 source-address 192.0.2.10
 destination-prefix 0.0.0.0/0
 static-address 198.51.100.50
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR supports IPsec for securing IP communications through encryption and authentication. Site-to-site VPNs use IKEv2 for key exchange and IPsec ESP for data protection. Configuration includes crypto keyrings for authentication, IKEv2 proposals and policies for phase 1, IPsec proposals and policies for phase 2, and crypto maps binding peers with traffic selectors.
cli_mode_context: Configure IPsec under 'crypto' hierarchy. Define IKEv2 keyring, proposal, policy, then IPsec proposal and policy. Create and apply crypto map to interface.
example_commands:
configure
crypto ikev2 keyring KEYRING-SITE-B
 peer 203.0.113.1
  address 203.0.113.1
  pre-shared-key Str0ngK3y123
crypto ikev2 proposal IKE-PROP
 encryption aes-cbc-256
 integrity sha256
 group 14
crypto ikev2 policy IKE-POLICY
 proposal IKE-PROP
crypto ipsec proposal IPSEC-PROP
 protocol esp encryption aes-256
 protocol esp integrity sha256
crypto ipsec policy IPSEC-POLICY
 proposal IPSEC-PROP
crypto map CMAP 10
 set peer 203.0.113.1
 set ikev2-policy IKE-POLICY
 set ipsec-policy IPSEC-POLICY
 match address ipv4 VPN-TRAFFIC
ipv4 access-list VPN-TRAFFIC
 10 permit ipv4 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255 198.51.100.0 0.0.0.255
interface TenGigE0/0/0/0
 ipv4 address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252

commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR QoS uses modular policy framework with class-maps for classification, policy-maps for actions, and service-policy for application to interfaces. QoS mechanisms include marking, policing, shaping, queuing, and scheduling. Hierarchical QoS (H-QoS) supports parent-child policies for complex traffic management. IOS-XR supports both ingress and egress QoS with hardware-based enforcement.
cli_mode_context: Define traffic classes with 'class-map', specify QoS actions in 'policy-map', and apply to interfaces with 'service-policy' in interface configuration.
example_commands:
configure
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any CRITICAL-DATA
 match dscp af31
class-map match-any BULK
 match dscp af11
policy-map CORE-OUT
 class VOICE
  priority level 1
  police rate percent 30
 class CRITICAL-DATA
  bandwidth percent 40
 class BULK
  bandwidth percent 20
 class class-default
  bandwidth percent 10
interface TenGigE0/0/0/1
 service-policy output CORE-OUT
commit
end

concept_summary: IOS-XR AAA provides centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting using TACACS+ or RADIUS servers. Task-based authorization controls which commands users can execute based on task IDs. AAA method lists define fallback sequences (server groups then local). Configuration supports per-user task assignments and command authorization at granular levels.
cli_mode_context: Configure AAA with 'aaa' commands in global config. Define server groups with 'tacacs-server host' or 'radius-server host', create method lists, and apply authorization task maps.
example_commands:
configure
tacacs-server host 192.0.2.50 port 49
 key TacacsSecret123
tacacs source-interface Loopback0
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
aaa authorization commands default group tacacs+ none
aaa accounting exec default start-stop group tacacs+
aaa accounting commands default start-stop group tacacs+
taskgroup OPERATOR
 task read aaa
 task read config-services
 task read ospf
 task read bgp
usergroup OPERATORS
 taskgroup OPERATOR
username operator
 group OPERATORS
 password Operater123
commit
end

Logging supports multiple destinations including console, buffer, and remote syslog servers with severity filtering. Syslog messages can be correlated with events for troubleshooting. Telemetry provides modern streaming data collection.

concept_summary: IOS-XR provides comprehensive EVPN support for data center and service provider use cases. EVPN uses BGP as control plane to distribute MAC/IP reachability information across MPLS or VXLAN networks. IOS-XR implements EVPN for E-LAN, E-Line, and E-Tree services with multihoming support via Ethernet Segment Identifier. EVPN-IRB enables inter-subnet routing with distributed anycast gateway.

interface TenGigE0/0/0/10.100 l2transport

  remote-as 65001

end

concept_summary: IOS-XR provides extensive MPLS capabilities for service provider networks including LDP for label distribution, RSVP-TE for traffic engineering, and Segment Routing for simplified MPLS. MPLS L3VPNs use VRFs with route distinguishers and route targets for customer separation. L2VPN services include pseudowires and VPLS for Layer 2 connectivity. IOS-XR supports advanced features like FRR, LFA, and TI-LFA for fast convergence.

concept_summary: IOS-XR provides carrier-grade high availability through redundant hardware and software mechanisms. NSR (Nonstop Routing) maintains protocol sessions during process restarts. ISSU (In-Service Software Upgrade) allows software upgrades without traffic disruption. Redundant route processors with SSO maintain control plane state. Graceful restart protocols (BGP GR, OSPF GR) enable hitless failover.

router bgp 65001

router isis CORE

commit
end
